When a query includes the shard key (or a prefix of a compound key) with equality or a range, mongos sends it only to the shards that own those values: a **targeted** query. Without the shard key, mongos must **broadcast** to every shard and merge the results (scatter-gather). That works, but latency is bounded by the slowest shard and load grows with shard count.

Other consequences of the shard key:
- Unique indexes on a sharded collection must have the shard key as a prefix (except `_id`, which is only guaranteed unique per shard if it is not the shard key).
- Updates and `findOneAndUpdate` that target a single document should include the shard key.
- Sorts across shards are merged by mongos; aggregations may push work to shards and merge on one.

Design the shard key from the top queries, just like indexes.

lesson.heading: Changing shard keys and zones
lesson.body:
Choosing a shard key used to be permanent. Modern MongoDB is more forgiving:

- 4.2: shard key **values** in a document can be updated (the document moves shards).
- 4.4: `refineCollectionShardKey` adds suffix fields to an existing key to increase cardinality.
- 5.0: `reshardCollection` changes the shard key entirely, rewriting data online with a short write block at the end.
- 8.0: collections can be unsharded or moved between shards.

Resharding is expensive (it copies the whole collection), so it is still worth choosing well up front.

**Zones** pin ranges of the shard key to specific shards, for example EU tenants to EU shards for data residency, or recent data to faster hardware. The key must start with the zoned field (such as `region`).

lesson.heading: Operational concerns
lesson.body:
- **Jumbo chunks**: ranges that grew too large to split because many documents share one shard key value. They cannot be migrated normally and cause imbalance. Prevention is a higher-cardinality key.
- **Balancer windows**: migrations consume I/O; schedule the balancer for off-peak hours on busy clusters.
- **Orphaned documents**: leftover copies after interrupted migrations; reads through mongos filter them out with the default read concern.
- **Pre-splitting**: for a bulk load into a new collection with a ranged key, pre-split and distribute ranges (or use hashed sharding, which can create initial ranges) to avoid all data landing on one shard.
- **Cross-shard transactions** work but involve two-phase commit, so keep data that changes together on the same shard by choosing the key (for example tenantId) accordingly.

keyPoints: A sharded cluster has shards (replica sets), mongos routers and config servers.
The shard key decides document placement; the balancer keeps ranges even.
Good shard keys have high cardinality, low frequency and non-monotonic writes, and match common queries.
Monotonically increasing ranged keys create a hot shard; hashed sharding spreads them.
Queries without the shard key are scatter-gather across all shards.
Unique indexes must be prefixed by the shard key.
Shard keys can be refined (4.4) or resharded (5.0+), but resharding is expensive.
Zones pin key ranges to shards for data residency or tiering.

questions.prompt: An events collection is sharded with ranged key { createdAt: 1 }. What problem appears under heavy insert load?
options: All new inserts go to the single shard owning the highest range (hot shard)
questions.explanation: A monotonically increasing ranged key sends every new document to the max range on one shard. Use a hashed key or a compound key with a high-cardinality prefix.

questions.prompt: The orders collection is sharded on { tenantId: 1, orderId: 1 }. Which query is targeted to a single shard (or a few)?
questions.explanation: Including the shard key prefix tenantId lets mongos route to the shards owning that tenant's range. orderId alone is not a prefix, so it is broadcast.

questions.prompt: What does mongos do?
options: Routes queries to shards using cluster metadata and merges results
questions.explanation: mongos is a stateless router. It caches routing metadata from config servers, sends operations to the right shards and merges results.

questions.prompt: A users collection is sharded on { country: 1 }. Most users are in one country. What is the main risk?
options: Jumbo ranges that cannot be split and an unbalanced cluster
Unique index on email becomes faster
questions.explanation: Low cardinality and high frequency mean many documents share one key value. A range for a single value cannot split, so it becomes jumbo and one shard holds most data.

questions.prompt: What is the main downside of hashed sharding on { _id: 'hashed' }?
options: Range queries on _id are broadcast to all shards
questions.explanation: Hashing destroys ordering, so adjacent values land on different shards. Equality queries are still targeted, but range queries must hit every shard.

questions.prompt: Which command changes a collection's shard key to a completely new key in MongoDB 5.0+?
questions.explanation: reshardCollection rewrites the collection with a new key online. refineCollectionShardKey can only add suffix fields to the existing key.

questions.prompt: You can create a unique index on email in a collection sharded on { tenantId: 1 } without including tenantId.
questions.explanation: Unique indexes on a sharded collection must be prefixed by the shard key, because each shard can only enforce uniqueness on its own data. { tenantId: 1, email: 1 } works.

questions.prompt: Each shard in a production sharded cluster is normally itself a replica set.
questions.explanation: Shards are replica sets so each portion of the data is highly available. Losing a shard's primary triggers an election within that shard only.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: properties of a good shard key are
options: Values that increase monotonically for ranged sharding
Low frequency of any single value
questions.explanation: High cardinality, low frequency and query alignment give even distribution and targeted queries. Monotonic values with ranged sharding cause hot shards.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: a query that does not include the shard key is sent to all shards, which is called a ___ query.
questions.explanation: mongos broadcasts the query and merges results. Latency depends on the slowest shard, and load grows with the number of shards.

questions.prompt: How would you choose a shard key for a multi-tenant SaaS orders collection?
questions.answer: I start from the queries: nearly every query is scoped to a tenant and often to a date range or order id. A compound key like { tenantId: 1, createdAt: 1 } or { tenantId: 1, _id: 1 } keeps each tenant's data together so queries are targeted and transactions within a tenant usually stay on one shard. tenantId alone has too little cardinality and large tenants would create jumbo ranges, so the second field adds cardinality. Within a tenant, createdAt is monotonic, but since writes are spread across many tenants the hot spot is limited; if one huge tenant dominates writes, I would consider a hashed suffix or isolate that tenant with zones. I would check that unique constraints can include tenantId as a prefix, and plan zones if tenants need data residency.

questions.prompt: When should you shard, and what should you try before sharding?
questions.answer: Shard when one replica set cannot handle the workload: the data or working set no longer fits on the largest practical machine, write throughput saturates a single primary, or you need geographic data placement. Before that I would fix queries and indexes, remove unused indexes, archive or TTL-expire old data, use projections and better schema design to reduce document size, scale vertically, and offload reads to secondaries where staleness is acceptable. Sharding brings operational cost: shard key design, balancing, scatter-gather queries, cross-shard transactions and more complex backups. In Atlas it is easier to operate, but the shard key decision remains the critical design step.

questions.prompt: Compare ranged and hashed sharding.
questions.answer: Ranged sharding divides the key space into contiguous ranges, so documents with nearby key values live together. Range queries and sorted scans on the key are efficient and targeted, and zones can pin ranges to shards. The risk is uneven writes when keys are monotonic or skewed. Hashed sharding distributes documents by a hash of the key, which spreads monotonically increasing keys like ObjectIds or timestamps evenly across shards and avoids hot spots. Equality lookups stay targeted, but range queries on the key become broadcast. A common compromise is a compound key with a hashed or high-cardinality component, or a ranged key whose prefix (like tenantId) spreads writes while preserving locality.

chapters.title: Atlas Search, Vector Search and Performance Tuning
chapters.summary: Add full-text and semantic vector search with $search and $vectorSearch, and tune MongoDB performance in production.

lesson.heading: Atlas Search
lesson.body:
**Atlas Search** embeds Apache Lucene next to the database. A separate search process (`mongot`) maintains search indexes that stay in sync with your collection automatically, so you do not need to run Elasticsearch and a sync pipeline yourself.

You query it with the `$search` aggregation stage, which **must be the first stage** of the pipeline. It supports analyzers and stemming, fuzzy matching for typos, `autocomplete`, phrase and wildcard queries, `compound` queries with `must`, `should`, `filter` and `mustNot` clauses, relevance scores, highlighting and faceted counts via `$searchMeta`.

The legacy `$text` operator with a text index is much more limited: no fuzzy matching, basic scoring, one text index per collection. For product search use Atlas Search (or an external engine).

lesson.heading: Vector search for semantic and RAG use cases
lesson.body:
**Vector search** finds documents whose embedding vectors are closest to a query vector, which captures meaning rather than exact words. You generate embeddings with a model (for example from Voyage AI, OpenAI or an open-source model), store them as an array field, and create a **vector search index** declaring the path, the number of dimensions and the similarity function (`cosine`, `euclidean` or `dotProduct`).

The `$vectorSearch` stage (also first in the pipeline) performs **approximate nearest neighbor** (ANN) search using an HNSW graph. `numCandidates` controls how many candidates are considered (higher is more accurate and slower; a common starting point is 10 to 20 times `limit`), and `exact: true` switches to exhaustive ENN search for small datasets. Pre-filters on fields indexed as `filter` type (such as `tenantId`) narrow the search.

Keeping vectors next to operational data is the main selling point for RAG apps: no separate vector database to sync. **Hybrid search** combines lexical `$search` and `$vectorSearch` results, for example with reciprocal rank fusion, to get both keyword precision and semantic recall.

lesson.heading: Working set, memory and storage engine
lesson.body:
MongoDB's storage engine is **WiredTiger**. It keeps hot data and indexes in its internal cache (by default 50 percent of RAM minus 1 GB, or 256 MB, whichever is larger) and relies on the OS file cache for the rest. Performance is best when the **working set** (frequently accessed documents and indexes) fits in RAM. When it does not, reads go to disk and latency jumps.

WiredTiger uses document-level concurrency control and compresses data (snappy by default; zstd and zlib available) and indexes (prefix compression).

Watch for: cache eviction pressure, growing index sizes, large documents where most fields are not read, and unbounded collections that should be expired with TTL or archived.

lesson.heading: Finding slow operations
lesson.body:
- The **database profiler** records operations slower than `slowms` (100 ms by default) at level 1, or all operations at level 2 (expensive; avoid in production). Results go to `system.profile`.
- Slow operations are also written to the server log.
- `db.currentOp()` shows running operations; `db.killOp()` stops a runaway one.
- `$indexStats` shows how often each index is used, so you can drop dead ones.
- In Atlas, the **Query Profiler**, **Performance Advisor** (index suggestions) and **Real-Time Performance Panel** surface the same data visually.

Always confirm a fix with `explain('executionStats')` before and after.

lesson.heading: Application-level tuning checklist
lesson.body:
- Reuse one `MongoClient` per process; the driver pools connections (`maxPoolSize` defaults to 100 in the Node.js driver). Tune it down for serverless instances.
- Return only needed fields with projections; use `.lean()` in Mongoose.
- Use range pagination instead of large `skip` values.
- Batch writes with `insertMany` / `bulkWrite` using `ordered: false` for independent writes.
- Avoid read-modify-write cycles; use atomic update operators.
- Avoid unbounded arrays and huge documents; apply subset, bucket and computed patterns.
- Set `maxTimeMS` on user-facing queries so a bad query cannot run forever.
- Choose write concern per use case; use secondaries for analytics with `secondaryPreferred` if staleness is acceptable, or dedicated analytics nodes.
- Use time series collections for metrics and events, and TTL indexes or online archive for old data.

keyPoints: Atlas Search is Lucene-based full-text search queried with $search, which must be the first pipeline stage.
Atlas Search supports fuzzy, autocomplete, compound queries, facets and relevance scoring; $text is far more limited.
$vectorSearch runs approximate nearest neighbor search over embedding vectors using a vector search index.
numCandidates trades accuracy for speed; filter fields must be indexed as filter type.
Performance depends on the working set (hot data plus indexes) fitting in the WiredTiger cache and RAM.
Use the profiler, slow query log, $indexStats and Atlas Performance Advisor to find problems.
Reuse one MongoClient, project fields, paginate by range and set maxTimeMS.

questions.prompt: Where must the $search stage appear in an aggregation pipeline?
questions.explanation: $search (and $vectorSearch) must be the first stage because they are executed by the search engine, which then feeds results into the rest of the pipeline.

questions.prompt: A user searches for 'iphnoe'. Which feature lets Atlas Search still find 'iphone'?
questions.explanation: Fuzzy matching allows a limited number of character edits (Levenshtein distance), so typos still match. A $text index cannot do this.

questions.prompt: What does increasing numCandidates in $vectorSearch do?
options: Considers more candidate vectors, improving recall at the cost of latency
questions.explanation: numCandidates is how many nearest neighbors the ANN search explores. limit controls how many are returned. More candidates means better accuracy and slower queries.

questions.prompt: In a multi-tenant RAG app, how do you ensure $vectorSearch only returns a tenant's documents?
options: Add a $match on tenantId after $vectorSearch only
Index tenantId as a filter field in the vector index and pass filter: { tenantId } in $vectorSearch
questions.explanation: A pre-filter restricts the ANN search to the tenant's vectors. Filtering only afterwards can return fewer than limit results and wastes work, and the field must be declared as a filter field in the index.

questions.prompt: What is the default slowms threshold for the database profiler and slow query log?
questions.explanation: Operations taking longer than 100 ms are considered slow by default and logged, or recorded in system.profile at profiler level 1.

questions.prompt: Latency spikes and disk reads rise sharply as a collection grows, while queries still use indexes. What is the most likely cause?
options: The working set no longer fits in RAM
questions.explanation: When hot data and indexes exceed the WiredTiger cache and OS cache, reads hit disk. Options include more RAM, smaller documents and indexes, archiving old data, or sharding.

questions.prompt: Atlas Search indexes are kept in sync with the collection automatically without you writing sync code.
questions.explanation: mongot tails changes from the database and updates Lucene indexes. They are eventually consistent, so a just-written document may take a moment to appear.

questions.prompt: Running the profiler at level 2 in production is a cheap way to capture every query.
questions.explanation: Level 2 records every operation, adding write load and storage. Use level 1 with a slowms threshold, sampling, or the Atlas profiler instead.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: which are valid similarity functions for an Atlas vector search index?
questions.explanation: Vector search indexes support cosine, euclidean and dotProduct. Use the one your embedding model was trained for; dotProduct requires normalized vectors.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: the aggregation stage for semantic similarity search over embeddings is ___.
questions.explanation: $vectorSearch runs ANN (or exact) search over a vector index and returns the closest documents with a vectorSearchScore.

questions.prompt: How would you build retrieval for a RAG chatbot on MongoDB?
questions.answer: Split source documents into chunks of a few hundred tokens with some overlap, and store each chunk as a document with its text, metadata (source, tenantId, updatedAt) and an embedding generated by a chosen embedding model. Create a vector search index on the embedding with the right numDimensions and similarity, plus filter fields such as tenantId. At query time embed the user question, run $vectorSearch with a tenant filter, a limit around 5 to 10 and numCandidates about 10 to 20 times higher, and project text plus score. For better relevance add hybrid search combining $search keyword results with vector results, and optionally a reranker. Re-embed chunks when content changes (a change stream can trigger this), and evaluate retrieval quality with a test set of questions.

questions.prompt: Your MongoDB-backed API got slow in production. Walk through your investigation.
questions.answer: I check whether it is all requests or specific endpoints, and correlate with deploys and traffic. On the database side I look at Atlas metrics or server stats: CPU, cache usage and eviction, disk IOPS, connections, replication lag and opcounters. Then I find the slowest query shapes in the profiler or slow query log and run explain on them for COLLSCAN, in-memory SORT and high docs-examined ratios. Common fixes are adding or reordering indexes (ESR), adding projections, replacing deep skip pagination, and removing N+1 query loops in the app. If the working set outgrew RAM, I archive or TTL old data, shrink documents, or scale up. I also check connection pool exhaustion, especially in serverless, and add maxTimeMS so one bad query cannot pile up.

questions.prompt: Compare Atlas Search with the $text operator and with running a separate Elasticsearch cluster.
questions.answer: $text uses a single text index per collection with basic stemming and scoring; there is no fuzzy matching, autocomplete or rich relevance tuning, so it suits only simple keyword search. Atlas Search uses Lucene and supports analyzers, fuzzy, autocomplete, synonyms, facets, highlighting and compound scoring, comparable to Elasticsearch for most app search needs. Compared to Elasticsearch it removes the sync pipeline and second cluster: indexes are updated automatically from the database and queried with aggregation, so you can combine search with $lookup and other stages. Elasticsearch may still win for log analytics, very custom scoring plugins or when search is a separate platform shared across many data sources. The tradeoff with Atlas Search is that it is eventually consistent and tied to MongoDB's platform.
